# SK2181 — `GetType()` is called on something that is already a `Type`

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

The receiver's static type is `System.Type`, so `GetType()` returns the runtime type of the `Type` object — `System.RuntimeType` — rather than the type it describes.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

`t.GetType()` where `t` is a `Type` answers a question nobody asked. It returns `System.RuntimeType` for every input, so the value is non-null, is a `Type`, and compares equal to itself — which is why it survives every test that checks for null and every test that checks two calls agree. The failure is silent and constant: a registry keyed on it has one key, a `switch` over it has one arm reachable, and a log line prints `RuntimeType` where a type name was meant. ⚠ **The compiler says nothing at all**, verified at `AnalysisMode=All`: `t.GetType()` and `typeof(Widget).GetType()` produce no diagnostic of any kind, and neither does any `CA*` rule.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
void Register(Type contract) {
    map[contract.GetType()] = contract;
}
```

Write:

```csharp
void Register(Type contract) {
    map[contract] = contract;
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Asking for the runtime type of a `Type` object is legitimate and is declined by recognising the question rather than by a name list.** Reflection-emit code distinguishes a `RuntimeType` from a `TypeBuilder`, a `TypeDelegator` or a mock, and it does so by comparing `t.GetType()` against a `typeof(...)` whose operand itself derives from `System.Type`. Wherever the call sits directly under a `==`, a `!=`, an `is` type pattern or an `is`/`as` operator naming such a type, the rule is silent — that author means exactly what they wrote. ⚠ **The receiver's *static* type decides, never the value.** `((object)t).GetType()` is the documented way to ask this question and is not reported, because the receiver is an `object` there; the rule does not look through the cast, and that is the escape hatch. A receiver typed `object`, `dynamic`, a type parameter, or an error type is declined for the same reason `SK2121` declines them: the conversion is classified against something other than the type that will be there. ⚠ **`fixIsSafe: false` although the edit is one deletion.** Removing `.GetType()` changes what the expression evaluates to — that is the whole finding — so it cannot be applied without a reader, and the fix is withheld entirely where a comment or a preprocessor directive sits inside the span being replaced. Generated code is excluded.
